lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: I have to ask, Trophonius—and you too, Amphilochus. You're dead. I don't know how you managed to get yourselves temples and a reputation as prophets, but the living are such idiots they actually think you're gods.

lines.speaker: Amphilochus
lines.text: Is it our fault if they’re stupid enough to worship corpses?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: They wouldn't worship you if you hadn't spent your lives pulling these stunts, pretending you could see the future and telling fortunes to anyone who asked.

lines.speaker: Trophonius
lines.text: Amphilochus can speak for himself, Menippus. But I am a hero. I give oracles to anyone who comes down to my shrine. You’ve obviously never been to Lebadea, or you wouldn't be questioning this.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: What? You mean if I didn't go to Lebadea, dress up in ridiculous linen robes, grab a barley-cake in each hand, and crawl on my belly through that tiny little hole into your cave, I couldn't possibly know that you're a corpse just like the rest of us, and your only real talent is fraud? But please, by your prophetic arts: what exactly is a 'hero'? I've always wondered.

lines.speaker: Trophonius
lines.text: A compound. Part man, part god.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: So it's neither man, as you say, nor god, but both at once? [pause] Where is this divine half of yours right now?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: I have absolutely no idea what you're talking about, Trophonius. But I can see perfectly well that you are entirely dead.
